reference.source: GeneReviews Refsum Disease / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Classic Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder of phytanic acid alpha-oxidation, usually from PHYH mutations and less often from PEX7 defects
The cardinal tetrad is retinitis pigmentosa, chronic peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar ataxia and raised cerebrospinal fluid protein without pleocytosis (albuminocytological dissociation)
Night blindness and progressively constricted visual fields from pigmentary retinopathy are often the earliest and most consistent feature
Additional clues include anosmia, sensorineural deafness, ichthyosis, skeletal abnormalities such as a shortened fourth toe, and cardiac conduction disturbance
Diagnosis rests on a markedly elevated plasma phytanic acid with normal or only mildly elevated very-long-chain fatty acids, distinguishing it from generalised peroxisomal disorders
Because phytanic acid is entirely of dietary (exogenous) origin, strict dietary restriction of phytanic acid, avoiding ruminant fats, dairy and certain fish, is the mainstay of treatment
Rapid weight loss and fasting mobilise phytanic acid from fat stores and can precipitate acute deterioration, so these are avoided; plasma exchange is used generically for acute severe episodes
reference.pathophysiology: Classic Refsum disease is a peroxisomal single-enzyme disorder in which deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (encoded by PHYH), or less commonly a defect of the peroxisomal targeting receptor PEX7, blocks the alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid. Phytanic acid is a branched-chain fatty acid derived exclusively from the diet, and because its beta-methyl group prevents beta-oxidation it must first undergo alpha-oxidation. When this pathway fails, phytanic acid accumulates in blood and lipid-rich tissues, where it is incorporated into membranes and disrupts myelin, retinal and neural function, producing the neuropathy, retinopathy and ataxia. Its wholly dietary origin is what makes dietary restriction effective.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of syndromic retinitis pigmentosa such as Usher and Bardet-Biedl syndromes
Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata (PEX7-related, with high phytanic acid)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma phytanic acid level, which is markedly elevated
Plasma pristanic acid and very-long-chain fatty acids to distinguish from generalised peroxisomal disorders
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing raised protein with normal cell count
Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography for pigmentary retinopathy
PHYH and PEX7 molecular genetic testing
redFlags: Cardiac arrhythmia or conduction block, a recognised cause of sudden death
Acute worsening of weakness or ataxia after fasting, illness or rapid weight loss
Rapidly progressive visual or hearing loss
Severe polyneuropathy compromising mobility or respiration
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and sustained dietary phytanic acid restriction the neuropathy and ataxia can stabilise or partially improve and progression slows, although retinopathy, deafness and anosmia tend to persist; untreated disease progresses and carries a risk of fatal cardiac complications.
pitfalls: Permitting rapid weight loss or fasting, which mobilises stored phytanic acid and can trigger acute deterioration
Failing to measure phytanic acid, so a treatable disorder is mistaken for another hereditary neuropathy or retinopathy
Overlooking cardiac conduction disease that requires monitoring
Not distinguishing classic Refsum disease from generalised peroxisomal disorders by checking very-long-chain fatty acids
management: Lifelong dietary restriction of phytanic acid, avoiding ruminant fats, dairy and certain fish, is the mainstay since phytanic acid is wholly dietary in origin
Maintain adequate caloric intake and avoid rapid weight loss or fasting, which mobilise phytanic acid from fat stores and can precipitate acute deterioration
Use plasmapheresis or lipid apheresis to rapidly lower phytanic acid in acute exacerbations or severe cardiac and neurological involvement
Provide dietitian-supervised nutrition with monitoring of plasma phytanic acid to guide dietary adjustment
Manage complications with cardiac conduction monitoring and pacing where needed, ophthalmology for the retinopathy, and support for neuropathy, ataxia, deafness and ichthyosis
Coordinate multidisciplinary specialist care and offer genetic counselling with family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
